t: LeetCode 1956 - Minimum Time for K Virus Variants to Spread
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Variant i occupies a cell from day manhattan(cell, origin_i) onward, expanding one Manhattan ring per day. We need the first day on which some single cell hosts at least k distinct variants - equivalently, minimize over lattice cells the k-th smallest Manhattan distance to the origins.

Examples:
- Origins (1,1) and (6,1) are 5 apart; their fronts meet halfway at day ceil(5 / 2) = 3.
- Origins (3,3), (1,2), (9,2): with k = 2 the answer is 2; with k = 3 it is 4.

Constraints are tiny (n <= 50, coordinates <= 100, so pairwise distances <= 198), which invites enumerating a modest box of candidate cells.
k: Restated: minimize, over all lattice cells, the k-th smallest Manhattan distance to the origin set.
The optimum lies inside the origins' bounding box expanded by about 200 per side: farther out, every distance already exceeds any achievable answer.
With at most roughly 600 cells per axis and n <= 50, brute force needs only tens of millions of elementary operations.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate Cells, Pick the k-th Smallest Distance
a.i: Any origin cell itself witnesses an answer of at most 198 (the grid diameter). A candidate more than 198 outside the bounding box is at distance greater than 198 from every origin simultaneously, so it cannot win. Expanding the box by 200 per side therefore suffices; evaluate each cell's distances and select the k-th smallest (partial selection or sort - n is tiny).
s: Compute min and max of x and y over the origins.
For each cell in the box expanded by 200, collect Manhattan distances to all origins.
Select the k-th smallest distance and update the global best.
a.t: O(B^2 * n log n) with B <= 600 - about 360k cells times 50 distances each

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search Plus Rotated-Square Sweep
a.i: Feasibility is monotone: if some cell sees k variants by day t it still does at t + 1, so binary search t. To test t, rotate to u = x + y, v = x - y: Manhattan balls become axis-aligned squares [u - t, u + t] x [v - t, v + t]; pre-scaling coordinates by 2 keeps every lattice cell on even (u, v), which means only even radii can change coverage - so binary search over even t and divide by 2 at the end. Some lattice point is covered by k squares iff on some candidate u line (square edges, now even) the active v-intervals overlap k-fold - checked with a sorted event sweep.
s: Scale every coordinate by 2 and map each origin to (u, v) = (x + y, x - y).
Binary search over even t in [0, 800].
For a candidate t build each square; for every square-edge u value gather the active v-intervals.
Sweep interval endpoints counting current coverage; reaching k proves feasibility.
Return the final lo divided by 2.
a.t: O(log(maxT) * n^2 log n) - about 10 probes, each sweeping at most 2n candidate lines with n intervals

w: Justify the transform aloud: after rotating 45 degrees, |dx| + |dy| becomes max(|du|, |dv|), turning diamonds into squares. Pitfalls: mixing metrics after the transform, forgetting duplicate origins (day 0 may already satisfy k), and forgetting to halve the scaled radius before returning. Follow-up: coordinates up to 10^9 kill cell enumeration and leave only the sweep-based approach.
